data.title: Pigmented purpuric dermatosis — viva
data.summary: Vascular & ulcers · 15 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Pigmented purpuric dermatosis** (Vascular & ulcers)_

**Q1. What are pigmented purpuric dermatoses (PPD)?**
- Group of chronic benign capillaritides — lymphocytic inflammation of superficial dermal capillaries with RBC extravasation and haemosiderin deposition, giving petechiae ('cayenne pepper' spots) on a brown background; mainly lower legs; not associated with systemic disease or platelet defects

**Q2. Name the clinical variants.**
- Schamberg's disease (progressive pigmentary purpura — commonest): irregular orange-brown patches with cayenne-pepper petechiae on shins/ankles of men
- Purpura annularis telangiectodes of Majocchi: annular patches with telangiectatic punctae, young women, legs
- Pigmented purpuric lichenoid dermatosis of Gougerot and Blum: lichenoid rust-brown papules coalescing into plaques, middle-aged men
- Lichen aureus: solitary golden-brown patch, often unilateral on leg/trunk, persistent, children/young adults
- Eczematid-like purpura of Doucas and Kapetanakis: itchy, scaly, eczematous, widespread
- Others: itching purpura of Lowenthal, granulomatous PPD (Asians), linear, transitory

**Q3. Aetiology / associations.**
- Mostly idiopathic; exacerbated by venous hypertension, exercise, standing, gravitational dependency
- Drugs: aspirin, NSAIDs, paracetamol, carbamazepine, furosemide, thiamine, glipizide, chlordiazepoxide, sildenafil, medroxyprogesterone; contact allergens (textile dyes, rubber, khaki clothing)
- Associations: diabetes, hyperlipidaemia (granulomatous variant), hepatitis C, rheumatoid arthritis; some persistent PPD can evolve into/mimic mycosis fungoides (clonal T cells)

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate around papillary dermal capillaries with endothelial swelling, extravasated RBCs and haemosiderin-laden macrophages (Perls' stain), no fibrinoid necrosis (not true vasculitis); lichenoid infiltrate in Gougerot–Blum and lichen aureus; spongiosis in eczematid type

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Stasis dermatitis/haemosiderosis (venous disease), drug-induced purpura, leukocytoclastic vasculitis (palpable), thrombocytopenic purpura, scurvy (perifollicular), MF (purpuric MF — biopsy, clonality), Kaposi sarcoma, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, cholesterol/hyperglobulinaemic purpura (Waldenström)

**Q6. Investigations.**
- Dermoscopy: red globules/dots over copper-orange background with brown network
- CBC with platelets, coagulation profile, blood sugar, lipids, LFT, HCV; review drugs; biopsy in atypical/persistent cases; TCR clonality if MF suspected

**Q7. Treatment.**
- Reassurance; stop suspect drugs; treat venous insufficiency (compression stockings, elevation)
- Topical steroids (moderate–potent) or tacrolimus for itch/inflammation
- Oral vitamin C 500 mg BD + rutoside (flavonoid) 50 mg BD — improves capillary fragility; pentoxifylline, griseofulvin, colchicine (case reports)
- NB-UVB/PUVA — particularly for widespread or MF-like disease
- Lasers (PDL) for cosmetically disturbing lesions

**Q8. Prognosis.**
- Chronic, relapsing–remitting over years; benign; pigmentation may persist; follow persistent widespread lesions for MF

**Q9. Describe lichen aureus in detail.**
- Solitary or few golden-brown to rust-coloured lichenoid patches/ plaques, often on legs, trunk, arms; children and young adults; persistent for years; may follow a perforator vein; dense band-like lymphocytic infiltrate with haemosiderin; treatment — topical steroids/ calcineurin inhibitors, PUVA

**Q10. What is granulomatous PPD?**
- Variant in Asians with PPD lesions and histological granulomas (perivascular histiocytes); associated with hyperlipidaemia — check lipids; resistant to therapy

**Q11. What is the role of venous insufficiency?**
- Raised venous pressure increases capillary fragility and extravasation; PPD lesions often limited to legs below knee in patients with varicose veins — compression and venous treatment help

**Q12. Describe the Gougerot–Blum variant.**
- Pigmented purpuric lichenoid dermatosis — small rust-brown lichenoid papules coalescing into plaques on legs of middle-aged men; dense lichenoid infiltrate — overlaps with lichen aureus; resistant; PUVA/ topical steroids

**Q13. Drug-induced PPD — mechanism and examples.**
- Hypersensitivity capillaritis to drugs: aspirin, paracetamol, NSAIDs, carbamazepine, furosemide, chlordiazepoxide, glipizide, medroxyprogesterone, thiamine, sildenafil, interferon; resolves after withdrawal (may take months)

**Q14. Why is PPD not a true vasculitis?**
- Histology shows lymphocytic capillaritis with extravasated RBCs and haemosiderin, but no fibrinoid necrosis of vessel walls or leukocytoclasia; lesions are non-palpable petechiae (except lichenoid variants) without systemic involvement

**Q15. What is the link with mycosis fungoides?**
- Persistent, extensive or lichenoid PPD can show clonal T cells and may coexist with or progress to MF (pigmented purpuric MF); biopsy with TCR gene rearrangement and follow-up in atypical, persistent cases

## Quick spotter facts
- Cayenne-pepper petechiae on orange-brown patches of shins — Schamberg's PPD
- Golden-brown solitary patch — lichen aureus
- Vitamin C + rutoside

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Pigmented purpuric dermatoses). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
